title: Siesta at the Lookout
text:
Only for your lips is my blood ripe,
with summer's obsession, prepared for your kisses,
always faithful to my arms and full of beauty—
my arms bloodless each night, unscathed at every dawn.

If the forests of hunting and adventure crackle
and the high birds mock us for being imprisoned,
do not let your eyes draw the bitterness
of those who have not carried love in their bones.

Stay between my arms, for you have only me,
while the others hate you, while the heart stalks you
in the warm beats of the belly
and of the temples.

See, there are no gardens beyond this wall,
which is all a long oblivion. And if my love holds you tight,
you will see an open sky behind
the dark weeping.

"Tigers in the Garden," 1968
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's intimate address, hunting and garden imagery, and the closing vision of sky behind dark weeping. Source tabs that visibly split single verse lines were folded; stanza breaks were retained.

title: Novalis
text:
Oh Night, how long since I have seen you so abundant
in stars and in fireflies, so drunk with perfumes.
After so many years I know you
in your blue fires, in your forests of chestnut and pine.
I know you in the fury of the barking dogs
and in the damp strawberries
that spring from the darkness.
I suspect you brimming with waterfalls and grapevines.

How long I have been silent, how much time I have lost,
how long I have dreamed, looking with eyes
washed with tears, as now, at your beauty.
My Night, do not cross this planet in vain.

Stop, spheres, and let the music grow fierce.
Night, sweetest Night,
since I must still return
to the world of men, let a star fall,
driving a burning harpoon between my sad eyes,
or let me reign in you like a moon.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Colinas's direct apostrophe to Night, the sensory catalogue of fires, forests, strawberries, and vines, and the final alternatives of wound or lunar sovereignty. Source tabs that visibly split single verse lines were folded; stanza breaks were retained.

title: Childhood Dream
text:
A clear night
of festivity and moonlight,
night of my dreams,
night of joy

—my soul was light
that today is all mist,
my hair was not
black yet—,

the youngest fairy
carried me in her arms
to the joyful festival
that blazed in the square.

Beneath the crackling
of the lights,
love wove its skeins
of dances.

And on that night
of festivity and moonlight,
night of my dreams,
night of joy,

the youngest fairy
kissed my brow…
with her lovely hand
she bade me farewell…

All the rosebushes
gave their fragrances,
all loves,
Love half-opened them.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Machado's refrain, the fairy's farewell, the poem's ellipses, and its movement from remembered light to present mist.

title: Elegy of a Madrigal
text:
I remember an afternoon of solitude and tedium,
oh, an afternoon like so many! My soul was,
beneath the monotonous blue, a broad, smooth river
that did not even have a poor reed bed on its bank.

Oh charmless world, sentimental poverty
that erases the mysterious quicksilver of the glass!
Oh loveless soul that the Universe copies
with an irrevocable universal yawn!

The poet wished to remember alone
the well-loved waves, the light of the hair
that he called blonde waves in his rhymes.
He read… The letter kills: he did not remember them…

And one day—as so many—while breathing in one day
the fragrances of a rose opening on the rosebush,
the light of the hair burst forth like a flame
that in his madrigals he called blonde waves;
it burst forth because they had had the same fragrance…
And he went away in silence to weep alone.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's self-correcting memory, the biblical echo in "The letter kills," the repeated "one day," and the return of fragrance as the trigger for remembered hair.

title: The Languid Lemon Tree Hangs...
text:
The languid lemon tree suspends
a pale, dusty branch
over the charm of the clear fountain,
and down there in the depths the golden fruits dream…
It is a clear afternoon,
almost spring;
a warm afternoon in March
that carries in its breath the nearness of April;
and I am alone, in the silent courtyard,
looking for a candid, old illusion:
some shadow on the white wall,
some memory asleep on the stone ledge
of the fountain, or, in the air,
some drifting of a light tunic.

In the afternoon air floats
that scent of absence
that says to the luminous soul: never,
and to the heart: wait.

That scent that calls up the ghosts
of virgin and dead fragrances.

Yes, I remember you, bright, happy afternoon,
almost spring,
flowerless afternoon, when you brought me
the good scent of spearmint,
and of sweet basil,
which my mother kept in her flowerpots.

Yes, you saw me plunge my pure hands
into the calm water,
to reach the enchanted fruits
that today dream at the bottom of the fountain…

Yes, I know you, bright, happy afternoon,
almost spring.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Machado's recurring invocation of the afternoon, the fountain's dreaming golden fruit, and the contrast between the soul's "never" and the heart's "wait."

title: The Flies
text:
You, familiar ones,
inevitable gluttons,
you, common flies,
you call all things to mind for me.

Oh old voracious flies
like bees in April,
old persistent flies
on my childish bald pate!

Flies of first tedium
in the family parlor,
the clear summer afternoons
when I began to dream!

And in the hated school,
swift, amusing flies,
chased
for love of what flies,

—for everything is flying—, sonorous
bouncing off the windowpanes
on autumn days…
Flies of every hour,

of childhood and adolescence,
of my golden youth;
of this second innocence,
which ends in believing in nothing,

of always… Common flies,
who, from being so familiar,
will have no worthy singer:
I know you have alighted

on the enchanted toy,
on the big closed book,
on the love letter,
on the dead eyelids
of the dead.

Inevitable gluttons,
who neither labor like bees,
nor shine like butterflies;
little restless ones,
you, old friends,
you call all things to mind for me.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the fly catalogue, the recurring familiar, gluttonous address, the wordplay on flying, and the final movement from childhood objects to the eyelids of the dead.

title: To a Dry Elm
text:
To the old elm, split by lightning
and half-rotten,
some green leaves have sprouted
with the April rains and the May sun.

The century-old elm on the hill
that the Duero licks! A yellowish moss
stains the whitish bark
of the worm-eaten, dusty trunk.

It will not be, like the singing poplars
that guard the road and the riverbank,
inhabited by brown nightingales.

An army of ants in file
climbs over it, and in its entrails
gray spiders weave their webs.

Before the woodcutter fells you, elm of the Duero,
with his axe, and the carpenter turns you
into a bell yoke,
a cart shaft, or a wagon yoke;
before tomorrow, red in the hearth,
you burn in some wretched hut
by the roadside;
before a whirlwind uproots you
and the breath of the white sierras snaps you;
before the river pushes you to the sea
through valleys and ravines,
elm, I want to note in my notebook
the grace of your newly green branch.

My heart waits
also, toward the light and toward life,
for another miracle of spring.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the elm's successive possible fates, the Duero and white sierras, and the speaker's final hope that the green branch foreshadows a miracle in his own heart.

title: Paths
text:
From the Moorish city
behind the old walls,
I contemplate the silent afternoon,
alone with my shadow and my sorrow.

The river runs
between shadowy orchards
and gray olive groves,
through the cheerful fields of Baeza.

The vines have golden leaves
over the red stocks.
Guadalquivir, like a broken
and scattered scimitar, glitters and mirrors itself.

Far away, the mountains sleep
wrapped in mist,
autumn mist, maternal; they rest,
the rough masses of their stony being,
in this warm afternoon of November,
a merciful, livid and violet afternoon.

The wind has shaken
the withered elms along the road,
lifting in pink whirlwinds
the dust of the earth.
The moon is rising, purplish, panting, full.

The little white paths
cross and draw away,
seeking the scattered farmsteads
of the valley and the sierra.
Paths of the fields…
Ah, now, I cannot walk with her!
editorial_note: The translation preserves Machado's solitary vantage, the maternal autumn mist, the broken-scimitar Guadalquivir, and the unresolved feminine pronoun in the final line.
